Grouped Random-Effect Term

Source: R/random.R
random.Rd

Random intercepts and slopes for a grouping factor: random(~ 1 | g) builds one coefficient per level of g, and random(~ x | g) one intercept and one slope per level, with the distribution of the effects attached as the penalty on those coefficients, which is how a random effect enters a penalized likelihood.

Usage

random(
  formula,
  distrib = NULL,
  correlated = TRUE,
  label = "random",
  hyper = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

formula

A bar formula, ~ lhs | g, with g evaluating to the grouping variable in the data, or ~ lhs | tag | g with a covariance label in the middle. g must not be continuous: a double carrying a value that is not a whole number is rejected, since its levels would be its formatted values.

distrib

The distribution of the effects: NULL (the default Gaussian), a distributions7 object, or a list of them with one per within-group column.

correlated

Logical; whether the default Gaussian lets the within-group effects correlate. Giving it together with distrib is an error, since distrib determines the same thing.

label

A single non-empty string prefixed to the coefficient names.

hyper

The hyperparameters of the effects' distribution to hold, as a named vector or list; those not named are estimated. For a distribution whose log-density has a kink, several values for one name are the grid that the path visits, and for any other distribution they are rejected. The names are the distribution's own parameters, with the within-group column appended where there is one copy per column. A name that the penalty does not carry is rejected when the term is built, which is where the penalty first exists.

id

Labels under which the effects' hyperparameters are shared with the hyperparameters of other terms carrying the same labels, so that two random effects may be given one variance component. The names are hyper's, checked at the same point and for the same reason; a single unnamed string is accepted where the effects' distribution carries one hyperparameter. NULL, the default, shares nothing. See term_ids().

...

Not used. A named argument is rejected with an error naming it, and the removed arguments precision and kinks are rejected with a message giving the replacement. An unnamed argument beyond those of the signature is rejected as well.

Value

An object of class RandomTerm() (a specification; see term_build()).

Details

The left side of the bar is an ordinary one-sided formula for the within-group design, with the usual intercept convention: ~ x | g carries an intercept and a slope per group and ~ 0 + x | g the slope alone. The block interacts that design with the group indicators, ordered group by group, so the coefficients of one group are adjacent.

The formula and the distribution of the effects determine the term. The parametrization in which the hyperparameters are estimated, their names, their number and the points where the log-density has a kink are all properties of that distribution, read from it at build time.

The covariance label, and the second bar

A formula may carry two bars, ~ 1 + x | u | g, following brms. The last position is the grouping variable and the middle one is a label: terms carrying the same label and the same grouping describe effects that are correlated with each other, so an intercept in one equation and a slope in another can share one covariance block. R nests bars to the left, so the parser itself yields that reading.

The label is a name and not data. It is read as a symbol and never evaluated, and a column of the data carrying the same name is not looked at, so ~ 1 | u | g builds the same block as ~ 1 | g, whatever u is.

A labelled term declares no penalty of its own. The covariance block spans columns that the term cannot see, possibly in another equation, so the prior over it belongs to the class and is built by the fitting layer. term_penalties() returns an empty list and term_penalty() is NULL. Consequently hyper and id are rejected when the term is built, the hyperparameters being those of the class, and a distrib given on a labelled term is the class's joint prior: it must be multivariate, and its dimension is checked where the class is known.

The two arguments have different scopes. correlated states whether the columns of this term may depend on each other, and the label states that its columns depend on those of other terms. The combination of correlated = FALSE with a label is contradictory and is rejected when the term is built.

The distribution of the effects

distrib is NULL, a distributions7 object, or a list of them with one per within-group column.

A multivariate distribution of the within-group dimension lets the effects of one group depend on each other, its matrix parameter carrying the dependence: mvgaussian2_distrib(2, ar1(2)) is a prior whose precision is autoregressive, mvstudent_t1_distrib(2) a heavy-tailed one. Correlated effects require a family that carries a matrix parameter, that is, a location block as long as the dimension together with a covariance, precision or scale matrix, and that defines the mixed response-parameter derivative block read by a marginal criterion. The term reads these properties from the family, so a family added later is covered without an edit here.

A univariate distribution makes the effects independent, the penalty being the product of the densities. With more than one within-group column it is a template: one copy per column, each with its own hyperparameters, since an intercept and a slope are quantities of different units and a shared scale would price them against each other. A list of distributions gives one per column explicitly, when the columns want different priors.

The default is Gaussian: gaussian1_distrib at one column, so the hyperparameter is the standard deviation of the effects; the multivariate Gaussian on an unstructured covariance when there are several columns and correlated = TRUE; and the template of the first when correlated = FALSE, with one standard deviation per column. The default has its location parameters held at zero.

A distribution supplied in distrib must have its location parameters held with distributions7::fixed(). A free location in the effects is confounded with the intercept of the equation in which the term sits, so a free location is rejected at build time with a message naming it. The value at which it is held is usually zero and is not checked, since the model is identified whatever the value is. Where the prior is a transformation of another family, the parameter is the mean on the original scale, so fixed(transformation(gamma2_distrib(), log_transform()), mu = 1) is a log-gamma prior with shape \(a = 1/\sigma^2\), where \(\sigma^2\) is the parameter sigma2 of the gamma. The mean of that prior, \(\psi(a) - \log a\), lies between \(-\sigma^2\) and \(-\sigma^2/2\) and tends to zero as \(\sigma^2\) tends to zero.

A distribution used as a penalty gives joint-mode (penalized likelihood) estimation of the effects. With Gaussian effects and a Gaussian response the Laplace approximation behind a marginal criterion is exact, so the variance component that the criterion returns is the marginal estimate. With any other prior the Laplace approximation is not exact, and modelterms7 does not compute the marginal likelihood.

The hyperparameters

They are the distribution's own free parameters, and every one of them is estimated unless it is held. There are two ways to hold one, and the fit is the same either way; what differs is what gets reported. Holding it inside the distribution, fixed(pseudohuber_distrib(), mu = 0, nu = 2), removes it: it becomes a constant of the prior and appears nowhere among the model's hyperparameters. Naming it in hyper keeps it, reported as held at the value given, as a penalized term's own hyperparameter argument does.

The hyperparameters of a prior with a smooth log-density are estimated by the outer criterion. A prior whose log-density has a kink, a Laplace or an elastic net, has none that a marginal criterion can reach, and its hyperparameter is chosen by a path over the sparse criterion of statmodels7::statmod(), statmodels7::bic() by default.

An estimated hyperparameter is reported with a standard error and an interval, a shape parameter included. The standard error is absent where the criterion at the point at which the run ended has a curvature of the wrong sign, since no interval follows from such a point. A shape parameter that moves toward a limit is the common case.

The parametrization of a family that is used as a prior matters. The centered skew normal (distributions7::skewnormal2_distrib()) carries the skewness itself, and its map to the direct parametrization is not twice differentiable at zero skewness. The derivatives of the log-density with respect to the skewness have a finite first-order limit there, and the second-order ones grow like \(\gamma_1^{-2/3}\). A marginal criterion reads the second-order ones, and the symmetric bounds place the starting value at that point, so the direct parametrization (distributions7::skewnormal1_distrib()) is the one to use as a prior; its derivatives at \(\alpha = 0\) are finite.

How well a shape parameter is estimated depends on the number of groups, since the parameter is read from that many latent values, which the prior shrinks. With few groups the estimate of a shape parameter can move to the Gaussian limit, and then only the scale is estimated. With more groups the estimate stays finite, but the criterion is flat over the small values, so the estimate locates the shape only to its order of magnitude. A shape parameter can be held with distributions7::fixed() when the number of groups is small, and an estimate from a moderate number of groups describes the weight of the tail without fixing its value. The \(\nu\) of a pseudo-Huber prior, the point at which the loss stops being quadratic, is subject to the same limitation.

Prediction maps new data onto the levels seen at build time. A level that the term has not seen, or a missing grouping value, is rejected by term_predict() unless unseen = "zero" is given, in which case the rows get no effect of their own.

A random effect is not standardized, and random() has no standardize argument; passing one is an error. Its columns are grouping indicators and its hyperparameter is a variance component with a meaning of its own. Dividing each coefficient by the spread of its indicator would weight the effects by the sizes of the groups, which changes the model itself.

The block and its penalty

With \(m\) levels and a within-group design \(Z_i\) of \(d\) columns, the block is the interaction of that design with the group indicators, ordered group by group. When the rows of the data are ordered by group, the block and the coefficient vector are

$$Z = \operatorname{diag}(Z_1, \dots, Z_m), \qquad b = (b_1', \dots, b_m')',$$

and otherwise the rows of this matrix are permuted to follow the data. The \(d\) coefficients of one group occupy adjacent positions and the penalty reads them one block at a time,

$$\rho(b; \theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^m \log f(b_i; \theta),$$

for the effects' density \(f\). Under the default Gaussian that is

$$\rho(b; \theta) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_i b_i'\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}b_i + \tfrac{m}{2}\log\lvert \Sigma(\theta)\rvert + \tfrac{md}{2}\log(2\pi),$$

and minimizing the penalized least squares in \((\beta, b)\) is the mixed-model equation at the variance ratio that \(\Sigma\) encodes, so the minimizer is the best linear unbiased predictor. At \(d = 1\) and \(\Sigma = \sigma_b^2\) it is the ridge, up to the constant that makes \(\sigma_b\) estimable.

Smooth random effects

Where the left side of the bar is an s() or a te() call, random(~ s(x) | g), each level of g has a random curve of its own (a random surface for te()), and the term is a RandomSmoothTerm(). With the smooth's columns split into the null space of its penalty \(N(x)\) and the penalized coordinates \(Z(x)\), group \(i\) contributes

$$g_i(x) = a_{0i} + N(x)a_i + Z(x)\delta_i, \qquad (a_{0i}, a_i) \sim \mathrm{N}(0, \Sigma), \qquad \delta_i \sim \mathrm{N}(0, \sigma^2 I),$$

independently over the groups. The null space is whatever the smoother's operator leaves unpenalized, less the constant: a straight line for a second-derivative penalty, a sine and a cosine for the harmonic operator, nothing for a cyclic smoother. The smoother's null_space decides what it contributes: under "keep" its columns carry \(\Sigma\) with the random level, under "shrink" they join the penalized coordinates, and under "drop" they are absent. ~ 0 + s(x) | g removes the random level.

\(\Sigma\) is the prior that distrib and correlated describe for the within-group columns of an ordinary random effect, here over the random level and the null space. With an unstructured \(\Sigma\) the model does not depend on the origin and the scale of x, nor on the phase of a periodic one. The penalized coordinates are whitened, so that their prior is independent with one standard deviation, reported as sigma of the entry smooth. A smoother with several smoothing parameters (an adaptive smoother, an anisotropic tensor product) keeps them: the precision is \(\sum_k \lambda_k S_k\) in every group, and the summary reports \(\lambda_k^{-1/2}\). All the groups share these hyperparameters, so the curves have one roughness. The population curve is a separate s() term in the same formula, as in y ~ s(x) + random(~ s(x) | g).

The smooth is written without by, sparse, hyper or id. The hyperparameters belong to the random effect, and hyper and id of this function name them (sigma.smooth, lambda1.smooth, ...). A covariance label between two bars is rejected.

References

Laird, N. M. and Ware, J. H. (1982). Random-effects models for longitudinal data. Biometrics 38, 963-974.

See also

s(), te(), nl()

Examples

dd <- data.frame(y = rnorm(9), x = rnorm(9),
                 g = factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c"), 3)))

# one variance component, reported as a standard deviation
term_penalty(term_build(random(~ 1 | g), dd))@params
#> [1] "sigma"

# intercepts and slopes, correlated: the covariance of the effects
built <- term_build(random(~ x | g), dd)
term_coef_names(built)
#> [1] "random.a.(Intercept)" "random.a.x"           "random.b.(Intercept)"
#> [4] "random.b.x"           "random.c.(Intercept)" "random.c.x"          
term_penalty(built)@params
#> [1] "sigma_log_L1" "sigma_log_L2" "sigma_L2.1"  

# independent, one standard deviation per column
vapply(term_penalties(term_build(random(~ x | g, correlated = FALSE), dd)),
       function(e) e$name, "")
#> [1] "(Intercept)" "x"          

# a heavy-tailed prior, held at four degrees of freedom
t4 <- distributions7::fixed(distributions7::student_t1_distrib(),
                            mu = 0, nu = 4)
term_penalty(term_build(random(~ 1 | g, distrib = t4), dd))@params
#> [1] "sigma"

# A covariance label, read from the middle of two bars and reported by
# term_tag(). It is a name: the block is the one bar formula's.
term_tag(random(~ 1 | u | g))
#> [1] "u"
identical(term_coef_names(term_build(random(~ 1 | u | g), dd)),
          term_coef_names(term_build(random(~ 1 | g), dd)))
#> [1] TRUE

# A continuous grouping variable is rejected rather than turned into one
# level per row.
try(term_build(random(~ 1 | x), dd))
#> Error : the grouping variable 'x' is continuous, and a grouping variable's
#>   values are labels rather than measurements: its levels would be the
#>   formatted numbers, one group per distinct value. Write factor(x) if
#>   they really are labels.

# A smooth random effect: one random curve per level of g.
sd <- data.frame(x = runif(60), g = factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c"), 20)))
rs <- term_build(random(~ s(x, smoother = basis7::bspline_smooth(k = 5)) |
                          g), sd)
term_group(rs)$names
#> [1] "(Intercept)" "lin"         "z1"          "z2"          "z3"         


# Fitted. The data are simulated from a known truth, so the
# estimates below can be read against it.
if (requireNamespace("statmodels7", quietly = TRUE)) {
  set.seed(6)
  fd <- data.frame(gr = factor(rep(1:20, each = 15)), x = rnorm(300))
  bb <- rnorm(20, sd = 0.8)
  fd$y <- 1 + 0.5 * fd$x + bb[fd$gr] + rnorm(300, sd = 0.5)
  cf <- coef(statmodels7::statmod(y ~ x + random(~1 | gr),
                                  distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), fd))$mu
  # truth: a slope of 0.5, and the shrunken effects track the ones drawn
  round(c(slope = cf[["x"]],
          cor = cor(cf[grep("^random", names(cf))], bb)), 3)
}
#> slope   cor 
#> 0.472 0.989
